title: Interior West birds moved upslope by about 84 m on fixed survey routes from 1981-1992 to 2012-2024 but did not move north; Pacific, Appalachian and Northeast birds did not move upslope
abstract: Question: in mountains, a 1 C cooler place is only 150-450 m higher but 150-400 km further north. If distance limits how closely species follow warming, birds should follow warming more closely upslope than northward. Approach: we used North American Breeding Bird Survey runs on fixed routes in four regions (Pacific, Interior West, Appalachians, Northeast) and three periods (1981-1992, 1995-2006, 2012-2024). For each species we fitted a smooth abundance profile in elevation, latitude and longitude and calculated the count change that an upslope or a northward shift would cause on each route. A conditional Poisson model with route and species fixed effects estimated both shifts together; route effects remove observer and route-wide changes. We used ETOPO1 route elevations, CRU TS May-July warming, a 2-degree block bootstrap, injection-recovery simulations, placebo year splits and 13 sensitivity variants. Results: in the Interior West (279 routes, 169 species) birds moved 84 m upslope (95% interval 43 to 86 m) and 5 km north (-17 to 16). The upslope shift repeated in 1981-1992 to 1995-2006 (+38 m) and 1995-2006 to 2012-2024 (+37 m), in the north and south of the region, and without first-year observers, burned routes or non-passerines. The isotherm shift was 214 m up and 220 km north, so the tracking ratios were 0.28 upslope and 0.03 north (difference 0.25, 0.09 to 0.37); after simulation calibration about 0.54 and 0.05. In the Pacific, Appalachians and Northeast, upslope shifts were -8 to +13 m with intervals across zero, and north shifts were also small; the Northeast moved 15 m downslope in 1995-2006 to 2012-2024. The pre-registered rule for the distance hypothesis (pooled and in 3 of 4 regions) was not met. Open-habitat species carried most of the Interior West shift (103 m against 30 m for forest species). Limitations: no detection model; coarse temperature and route elevation; calibration depends on simulated noise; drought, low-elevation habitat change and fire severity were not separated from warming.
